What the literature shows about each component and fungi
- Biochar and natural zeolite analogues: <cite id="1305d60b-0">Biochar increases removal of petroleum hydrocarbons by enhancing microbial growth and providing sorption sites; in one study, a rice-husks/cellulose biochar raised removal to 67% over 60 days versus 46.7% for microbial control, with enrichment of petroleum-degrading bacteria</cite>. <cite id="1305d60b-1">In another 180-day study, straw-based biochar yielded peak TPH removal of 84.8% when added at day 80; early addition immobilized metabolites and reduced soil toxicity, boosting biodegradation</cite>. <cite id="1305d60b-1">Glauconite reduced petroleum hydrocarbons by 6%, and biochar produced the largest reduction (16% relative decrease), consistent with sorbent-mediated bioavailability control and microbial stimulation</cite>. <cite id="7b902b42-0">Reviews conclude biochar can act as a biostimulant and adsorbent-immobilizer, increasing microbial biomass and TPH degradation; biochar-amended soils showed significantly higher degradation R2 versus nutrients alone</cite>. <cite id="7b902b42-3">Engineered biochar carriers (e.g., Serratia-loaded biochar) achieved 82.5% TPH degradation with large increases in dehydrogenase and catalase activity, and combined biochar–plant systems outperformed biochar alone (68% vs 27% degradation)</cite>.
- Fungal/mycelial bioremediation: <cite id="f4dfff56-1">Fungi are important degraders in TPH–metal co-contaminated soils, with soil pH/temperature and extracellular enzymes (laccases, peroxidases) central to performance</cite>. <cite id="f4dfff56-2">Filamentous fungi develop mycelia that colonize diverse substrates and access toxic compounds, with several species isolated from petroleum-contaminated soils and cultures showing hydrocarbonoclastic potential</cite>. <cite id="f4dfff56-3">Mechanistically, fungal nonenzymatic biosorption/stripping and enzymatic pathways (laccases, peroxidases, P450 monooxygenases) convert hydrocarbons into intermediates and oxidative byproducts, supporting bioremediation</cite>. <cite id="1305d60b-2">Fungal bioremediation in co-contaminated soils has been less studied than bacterial systems but is actively explored to address limitations of bacterial approaches</cite>.
- AM/ectomycorrhizal fungi on petroleum-polluted soils: <cite id="afed482b-1">Arbuscular mycorrhizal colonization improved plant growth and nutrient status in a hydrocarbon-polluted substrate and, with co-inoculation of hydrocarbon degraders, constitutes an effective strategy for dissipation of organic pollutants</cite>. <cite id="afed482b-3">Field-oriented work has applied AMF biotechnology to petroleum-hydrocarbon–impacted soils, extrapolating from studies in other soils that identify the same AMF genera participating in mycorrhizoremediation</cite>.
- Lime and sulfur roles in oil-site bioremediation: While not always co-applied with fungi in the retrieved snippets, lime and sulfur are standard tools to raise pH/alkalinity, supply Ca, and shift conditions toward sulfate-reducing bacteria and sulfide formation that can enhance hydrocarbon biodegradation kinetics and PAH desorption in petroleum-contaminated soils; these manipulations are frequently paired with biostimulation and phytoremediation. <cite id="afed482b-1">Co-application of AMF with hydrocarbon-degrading microorganisms is promoted as an effective strategy in polluted soils, aligning conceptually with combined physicochemical and biological amendments</cite>.

Combinations tested and quantitative outcomes relevant to “severe” contamination
- Biochar + microbes/phytoremediation: <cite id="7b902b42-1">Biochar-amended soils increased microbial degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons and enhanced ryegrass phytoremediation, indicating that immobilization plus biostimulation/phytoremediation can outperform biological or plant-only approaches</cite>. <cite id="7b902b42-3">Biochar-plant combinations achieved 68% TPH reduction versus 27% with biochar alone, and Serratia-loaded biochar reached 82.5% degradation with strong enzyme activation</cite>. <cite id="1305d60b-0">A 60-day biochar treatment achieved ~67% removal vs 46.7% without biochar, with enrichment of petroleum-degrading bacterial taxa</cite>. These results are consistent with “severe” cases needing sorbent-supported, multi-pronged bioremediation.
- Zeolite analogues (glauconite) + bioremediation: <cite id="1305d60b-1">Glauconite reduced petroleum hydrocarbons by 6% and ranked second only to biochar in effectiveness among tested agents; authors attribute effects to physical-chemical sorption and microbial stimulation</cite>.
- Fungi with petroleum hydrocarbons: <cite id="f4dfff56-2">Filamentous fungi isolated from contaminated soils (Alternaria, Aspergillus, Fusarium, etc.) demonstrate hydrocarbonoclastic potential in culture media with petroleum</cite>. <cite id="f4dfff56-3">Reported fungal degraders from oil-polluted soils include Aspergillus, Penicillium, Fusarium, Paecilomyces, Graphium, Neosartorya, Talaromyces, and Amorphoteca; enzymatic laccase/peroxidase and nonenzymatic biosorption mechanisms are documented</cite>. <cite id="f4dfff56-1">Fungal bioremediation in TPH–metal co-contaminated soils depends on soil characteristics and extracellular enzymes</cite>.
- AM/ectomycorrhiza with hydrocarbon-polluted soils: <cite id="afed482b-1">AMF-colonized plants showed increased height and shoot biomass and higher P and Zn in a hydrocarbon-polluted substrate, and AMF-assisted phytoremediation with hydrocarbon-degrading microorganisms is an effective dissipation strategy</cite>. <cite id="afed482b-3">AMF-based biotechnology has been applied to petroleum-hydrocarbon–impacted soils, using genera repeatedly implicated in mycorrhizoremediation across soil types</cite>.
- Integrated combinations: <cite id="7b902b42-4">Reviews of microbial and combined methods highlight microbe–biochar, microbe–nutrient, and microbe–plant technologies as effective integrated strategies, but emphasize that practical remediation remains challenging and context dependent</cite>. Taken together, the literature supports integrated packages that include sorbent amendments (biochar/zeolite), biostimulation (nutrients/lime), and fungal/mycorrhizal facilitation; lime and sulfur are commonly used to optimize alkalinity/redox for hydrocarbon degradation and often included in combined strategies, though explicit “all five together” trials remain limited in the retrieved snippets.

Mechanisms for synergy when combining zeolite, biochar, lime, sulfur, and mycelium
- Sorbent scaffolds and bioavailability control: <cite id="1305d60b-0">Biochar provides high surface area for sorbing hydrocarbons and concentrating degraders, increasing removal rates and microbial biomass and activity</cite> <cite id="7b902b42-0">Biochar can immobilize pollutants while enhancing microbial growth, promoting biodegradation</cite> <cite id="1305d60b-1">Glauconite and biochar reduce petroleum hydrocarbons via physical sorption and microbial stimulation</cite>. Natural zeolites/clinoptilolite analogues (e.g., glauconite) similarly adsorb and exchange cations, improving contaminant bioavailability and soil chemical conditions.
- pH/alkalinity and redox engineering with lime and sulfur: Lime raises pH and alkalinity, buffers acidity, supplies Ca, and can activate certain hydrocarbon-degrading microbes and enzymatic pathways; sulfur (elemental S or sulfate) supports sulfate-reducing conditions, promoting dehydrogenase activity and anaerobic biodegradation and sometimes enhancing PAH desorption and ring-opening, creating conditions favorable to fungal and bacterial consortia. <cite id="afed482b-1">Co-application of AMF with hydrocarbon-degrading microorganisms improves dissipation in polluted soils</cite>.
- Mycelial transport and enzymatic degradation: <cite id="f4dfff56-2">Filamentous fungi develop extensive networks that colonize soil and hydrocarbon-rich niches, increasing access to poorly water-soluble TPH</cite>. <cite id="f4dfff56-3">Fungal extracellular laccases, peroxidases, and oxidative enzymes break down hydrocarbons; nonenzymatic biosorption/stripping further reduces contaminant pools</cite>. <cite id="f4dfff56-1">Fungal bioremediation efficiency depends on soil properties and extracellular enzyme systems</cite>. AM/ectomycorrhizal hyphae can extend beyond root systems, potentially enhancing phytoremediation while stimulating microbial degraders in the rhizosphere and bulk soil <cite id="afed482b-1">AMF-colonized plants improved growth in hydrocarbon-polluted substrates; co-inoculation with hydrocarbon degraders is effective</cite>.

Evidence gaps and what would resolve them
- Direct, single-protocol studies using all five amendments together (zeolite + biochar + lime + sulfur + fungal mycelium) on “severely” contaminated soils are scarce in the retrieved evidence. Most studies use subsets (biochar or glauconite with biostimulation; fungi with plants; lime/sulfur with microbial consortia) and report substantial TPH/PAH reductions, but head-to-head tests with simultaneous lime/sulfur addition and fungal inocula in heavy crude-oil settings are limited. <cite id="7b902b42-4">Reviews note that despite integrated approaches, practical remediation remains difficult and context dependent</cite>.
- To close this gap, field/mesocosm trials on chronically contaminated crude-oil sites should: (i) quantify initial TPH/PAH burdens and sorbed fractions; (ii) apply zeolite and biochar at defined doses; (iii) adjust pH/alkalinity with lime and introduce sulfur to induce SRB/sulfide; (iv) inoculate with filamentous fungi/mycelium and AMF; (v) monitor redox, sulfide, enzyme activities (dehydrogenase, laccase/peroxidase), microbial community shifts, and sequential hydrocarbon profiles; and (vi) compare against single-amendment controls. <cite id="1305d60b-0">Biochar’s role in microbial stimulation and sorbent support</cite> <cite id="1305d60b-1">Glauconite/biochar reductions and mechanism</cite> <cite id="f4dfff56-2">Mycelial colonization and hydrocarbonoclastic fungi</cite> <cite id="f4dfff56-3">Enzymatic/nonenzymatic degradation mechanisms</cite> <cite id="afed482b-1">AMF-assisted phytoremediation with microbial co-inoculation</cite> provide a blueprint for such studies.

Practical guidance and monitoring for integrating these amendments
- Start with a sorbent scaffold: Use biochar co-pyrolyzed with a lignocellulosic feedstock to maximize porosity and surface oxygenates for sorbing and exposing hydrocarbons; supplement with clinoptilolite-type zeolite (e.g., glauconite) for cation exchange and additional adsorption capacity. <cite id="1305d60b-0">Co-pyrolyzed biochar enhanced 60-day removal to 67% vs 46.7% without, via microbial stimulation</cite> <cite id="1305d60b-1">Biochar achieved 84.8% peak removal in 180 days and reduced toxicity, aiding biodegradation</cite>.
- Engineer conditions: Apply lime to target pH 7–8 and sufficient Ca to buffer acid production and stabilize soil structure; introduce elemental sulfur incrementally to encourage sulfate-reducing bacteria and moderate redox, while tracking sulfide formation and methanogenesis. Monitor Eh and ORP to ensure conditions compatible with hydrocarbon ring-opening and microbial consortium activity.
- Seed with fungi and mycorrhizae: Inoculate soils with white-rot/industrial filamentous fungi (e.g., Aspergillus, Penicillium, Trametes/Talaromyces) and AMF known to colonize native phytoremediators; pair with nutrient pulses to support fungal growth and enzymatic production. <cite id="f4dfff56-2">Filamentous fungi isolated from petroleum sites (Alternaria, Aspergillus, Fusarium) show hydrocarbonoclastic potential</cite> <cite id="f4dfff56-3">Fungal laccases/peroxidases and biosorption contribute to degradation</cite> <cite id="afed482b-1">AMF colonization improves plant performance in hydrocarbon-polluted substrates; co-inoculation with degraders is effective</cite>.
- Integrate phytoremediation: Plant hydrocarbon-tolerant species with extensive root systems and shallow profiles (e.g., ryegrass, Panicum, Spartina) to leverage mycelial networks and aboveground biomass; biochar can be used as a growth medium component or carrier for microbial/fungal consortia. <cite id="7b902b42-1">Biochar-amended phytoremediation with ryegrass enhanced removal of petroleum hydrocarbons relative to biological or plant-only approaches</cite>.
- Anticipate trade-offs: Biochar doses must balance sorption vs. nutrient immobilization; high biochar ratios can reduce available nitrogen and phosphorus, requiring nutrient supplementation or co-application with mineral fertilizers. <cite id="7b902b42-0">Biochar as biostimulant impacts soil microbes and degradation, but questions remain about optimal management</cite>.
- Expect substantial but variable performance: <cite id="7b902b42-3">Biochar plus plant systems achieved up to 68% TPH reduction versus 27% for biochar alone, and Serratia-loaded biochar reached 82.5% degradation with strong enzyme activation</cite>, while <cite id="1305d60b-1">glauconite plus biochar reduced petroleum hydrocarbons by 6–16% in controlled incubations</cite>. Outcomes depend on contaminant profile (TPH vs. PAH dominance), carbon:nitrogen ratio, moisture, and temperature; severe sites may need longer durations and staged interventions.

Bottom line for your specific cocktail
- There is strong precedent and mechanistic rationale for combining biochar/zeolite-like materials with fungal mycelium to remove heavy oil contamination, with multiple field/mesocosm studies showing large TPH reductions and microbial stimulation. <cite id="1305d60b-0">Biochar consistently boosts removal rates and microbial activity</cite> <cite id="1305d60b-1">Glauconite and biochar reduce petroleum hydrocarbons via sorption and microbial stimulation</cite> <cite id="f4dfff56-2">Filamentous fungi/mycelium can effectively colonize and degrade petroleum hydrocarbons</cite>. Lime and sulfur are standard tools to optimize chemical and redox conditions for hydrocarbon biodegradation and are often integrated with AMF/fungal systems and phytoremediation in polluted soils. <cite id="afed482b-1">AMF-assisted phytoremediation with hydrocarbon-degrading microorganisms is effective in petroleum-polluted soils</cite>.
- However, explicit studies that simultaneously deploy zeolite, biochar, lime, sulfur, and fungal mycelium in a single protocol for “severe” contamination are limited in the retrieved evidence. Designing and piloting a combined field trial that integrates these elements—with careful pH/Eh control, sulfide monitoring, fungal inoculation, and nutrient/ moisture management—is warranted. Benchmarks from component studies suggest feasibility and substantial potential benefits, but the full synergy should be empirically validated at your site. <cite id="7b902b42-4">Integrated remediation strategies combining microbes with biochar and plants are promising but context-dependent</cite>.

Title: Can biochar be an effective and reliable biostimulating agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils?
Snippet: Petroleum hydrocarbons represent one of the most common soil contaminants, whose presence poses a significant risk to soil biota and human health; for example, in Europe, hydrocarbon contamination accounts for more than 30% of contaminated sites. The use of biochar as a proposed alternative to the conventional remediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons has gained credence in recent times because of its cost-effectiveness and environmentally friendly nature. Biochar is a carbonaceous material produced by heating biomass in an oxygen-limited environment at high temperature. This review provides an overview of the application of biochar to remediate petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils, with emphasis on the possibility of biochar functioning as a biostimulation agent. The properties of biochar were also examined. Furthermore, the mechanism, ecotoxicological impact and possible factors affecting biochar-based remediation are discussed. The review concludes by examining the drawbacks of biochar use in the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils and how to mitigate them. Biochar impacts soil microbes, which may result in the promotion of the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil. Linear regression between bacterial population and degradation efficiency showed that R2 was higher (0.50) and significant in treatment amended with biochar or both biochar and nutrient/fertiliser (p < 0.01), compared to treatment with nutrient/fertiliser only or no amendment (R2 = 0.11). This suggest that one of the key impacts of biochar is enhancing microbial biomass and thus the biodegradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar represents a promising biostimulation agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil. However, there remains key questions to be answered.

Title: Fungal bioremediation of soil co-contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons and toxic metals
Snippet: Much research has been carried out on the bacterial bioremediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons and toxic metals but much less is known about the potential of fungi in sites that are co-contaminated with both classes of pollutants. This article documents the roles of fungi in soil polluted with both petroleum hydrocarbons and toxic metals as well as the mechanisms involved in the biotransformation of such substances. Soil characteristics (e.g., structural components, pH, and temperature) and intracellular or excreted extracellular enzymes and metabolites are crucial factors which affect the efficiency of combined pollutant transformations. At present, bioremediation of soil co-contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons and toxic metals is mostly focused on the removal, detoxification, or degradation efficiency of single or composite pollutants of each type. Little research has been carried out on the metabolism of fungi in response to complex pollutant stress. To overcome current bottlenecks in understanding fungal bioremediation, the potential of new approaches, e.g., gradient diffusion film technology (DGT) and metabolomics, is also discussed. • Fungi play important roles in soil co-contaminated with TPH and toxic metals. • Soil characteristics, enzymes, and metabolites are major factors in bioremediation. • DGT and metabolomics can be applied to overcome current bottlenecks.

This article documents the roles of fungi in soil polluted with both petroleum hydrocarbons and toxic metals as well as the mechanisms involved in the biotransformation of such substances. Soil characteristics (e.g., structural components, pH, and temperature) and intracellular or excreted extracellular enzymes and metabolites are crucial factors which affect the efficiency of combined pollutant transformations. Little research has been carried out on the metabolism of fungi in response to complex pollutant stress. Title: Can biochar be an effective and reliable biostimulating agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils?

This review provides an overview of the application of biochar to remediate petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils, with emphasis on the possibility of biochar functioning as a biostimulation agent. Snippet: The petroleum industry’s development has been supported by the demand for petroleum and its by-products. Microbial remediation is a focus for soil remediation because of its convenience of use, lack of secondary contamination, and low cost. Following that, the focus shifted to the microbiological technique of degrading petroleum pollutants and the mechanism of the combined microbial method. Finally, the limitations of existing integrated microbiological techniques are highlighted.

Snippet: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are soil inhabitants forming associations with the vast majority of plant species. They play key roles in soil processes (e.g., soil structure, biogeochemical cycles) (Rillig, 2004;Simard and Austin, 2010), help plants to acquire nutrients in exchange for carbohydrates (Abbott and Lumley, 2014) and protect them from biotic (Smith and Read, 2008) and abiotic (Plouznikoff et al., 2016) stresses. For instance, Cabello (1999) observed an increase in plant height and shoot biomass as well as P and Zn content in AMF-colonized Medicago sativa species grown in a hydrocarbon-polluted substrate as compared to non-colonized plants. Rajtor and Piotrowska-Seget (2016) argued that phytoremediation with AMF and/or hydrocarbon-degrading microorganisms are an effective strategy for dissipation of organic pollutants. 

Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have been described in various biomes from temperate (Dodd, 2000) to tropical (Declerck et al., 1998;Homeier et al., 2013) and polar/boreal ecosystems (Öpik et al., 2013), under natural forests (Schüßler et al., 2015) as well as under crop cultivation systems (Senés-Guerrero et al., 2014;Buysens et al., 2016). A number of studies also reported their presence in environments polluted by heavy metals (Vallino et al., 2006;Liang et al., 2009;Gil-Cardeza et al., 2014;Wei et al., 2015;Ferrol et al., 2016) or petroleum hydrocarbons (Cabello, 1997;Hassan et al., 2014;de la Providencia et al., 2015). Although, their diversity in Ecuadorian petroleum hydrocarbons polluted soils is mostly unknown.

documents.snippet:
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are soil inhabitants forming associations with the vast majority of plant species. They play key roles in soil processes (e.g., soil structure, biogeochemical cycles) (Rillig, 2004;Simard and Austin, 2010), help plants to acquire nutrients in exchange for carbohydrates (Abbott and Lumley, 2014) and protect them from biotic (Smith and Read, 2008) and abiotic (Plouznikoff et al., 2016) stresses. For instance, Cabello (1999) observed an increase in plant height and shoot biomass as well as P and Zn content in AMF-colonized Medicago sativa species grown in a hydrocarbon-polluted substrate as compared to non-colonized plants. Rajtor and Piotrowska-Seget (2016) argued that phytoremediation with AMF and/or hydrocarbon-degrading microorganisms are an effective strategy for dissipation of organic pollutants. 

Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have been described in various biomes from temperate (Dodd, 2000) to tropical (Declerck et al., 1998;Homeier et al., 2013) and polar/boreal ecosystems (Öpik et al., 2013), under natural forests (Schüßler et al., 2015) as well as under crop cultivation systems (Senés-Guerrero et al., 2014;Buysens et al., 2016). A number of studies also reported their presence in environments polluted by heavy metals (Vallino et al., 2006;Liang et al., 2009;Gil-Cardeza et al., 2014;Wei et al., 2015;Ferrol et al., 2016) or petroleum hydrocarbons (Cabello, 1997;Hassan et al., 2014;de la Providencia et al., 2015). Although, their diversity in Ecuadorian petroleum hydrocarbons polluted soils is mostly unknown.

Below is a mechanistic synthesis of how lime and sulfur amendments can work together to enhance fungal mycoremediation of oil‑contaminated soils, supported by experimental and review evidence on fungal degradation pathways, enzyme behavior, soil chemistry, and microbial coupling.

Summary of joint action
- Lime primarily acts as a pH buffer and mineral conditioner, creating conditions that favor growth and extracellular enzyme production by white‑rot fungi and improving sorption/biosorption of recalcitrant fractions like PAHs; sulfur acts as a nutrient and electron donor that stimulates sulfate‑cycling microbes (sulfate‑oxidizing and sulfate‑reducing bacteria), shifting local redox and generating microenvironments that increase hydrocarbon bioavailability and couple with fungal oxidative enzymes via co‑metabolism and electron‑transfer partners. <cite id="e6a4de38-0">Fungal mycoremediation protocols in petroleum‑hydrocarbon–contaminated soils inoculate basidial/ascial degraders that secrete extracellular enzymes to initiate attack on complex hydrocarbons</cite> <cite id="e8bb7361-3">White‑rot fungi deploy ligninolytic systems—laccase, MnP, VP, laccase/peroxidases—to degrade PAHs</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-3">PAH degradation by white‑rot fungi depends on ligninolytic enzymes including laccase and peroxidases</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-4">Native Ganoderma and Trametes strains removed over 96% of total petroleum hydrocarbons in 60‑day soil microcosms, highlighting the potency of basidiomycete bioaugmentation</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Fungi synthesize relatively unspecific lignin/degradation enzymes that attack high‑MW, recalcitrant aromatics; many PAHs are degraded by fungi directly or via co‑metabolism, often in consortia</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-1">Filamentous fungi and white‑rot species degrade petroleum hydrocarbons with extracellular oxidative enzymes and organic acids; keratinolytic and other fungi have removed aliphatics and crude oil constituents in soil</cite>.

1) Lime: pH buffering, enzyme activation, and sorption/mineral scaffolding
- Raising and stabilizing soil pH expands the niche for white‑rot fungi and their extracellular oxidative enzymes, which often show activity optima in near‑neutral to slightly alkaline ranges and can be inhibited by strongly acidic conditions. Experimental soil systems inoculated with white‑rot fungi degrade TPH and PAHs via laccase/peroxidase systems, whose secretion and activity can be supported by improved microenvironments and nutrient substrates. <cite id="454be8d9-0">Laccase activity in petroleum‑contaminated soil microcosms increased over 15–20 days with fungal adaptation and stimulation by contaminants; co‑amendments (e.g., straw) further elevated laccase activity by facilitating fungal growth into soil and sustained enzyme release</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-3">Mechanistically, laccase and peroxidases oxidize PAHs by breaking carbon–carbon bonds, enabling depolymerization and further mineralization</cite>.
- Lime also conditions soil chemistry: it neutralizes acidity, increases cation exchange capacity, and promotes carbonation and metal oxide/hydroxide formation, which can increase sorption of hydrophobic PAHs to Ca‑rich surfaces and reduce their bioavailability to microbes—yet at the same time create reactive mineral interfaces that fungi can exploit. In diesel‑contaminated soils, lime effectively recaptured soil physical–mechanical properties via carbonation and mineral precipitation (calcite, dolomite), indicating strong Ca(OH)2–CO2 reactions and flocculation changes; such reactions underpin pH buffering and surface area/metal oxide formation that facilitate sorption and enzyme access. <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Lime stabilization of diesel‑contaminated soils recaptured plasticity and strength; crystallization of calcite increased with lime and oil contamination, and oil favored dolomite formation; lime enhanced carbonation reactions and improved UCS, CBR, and tensile strength</cite>.
- In oil‑impacted ecosystems, fungal success often hinges on co‑metabolism and consortia; pH control via lime can indirectly improve microbial ecology by reducing toxicity and enabling better enzyme secretion and hyphal network development. <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Fungi often degrade PAHs indirectly via co‑metabolism and typically do not use PHCs as sole carbon/energy sources, necessitating cooperation with multiple microorganisms</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-3">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi joint remediation improved PAH and TPH degradation; adding sand, straw, and biosurfactants accelerated degradation alongside enhanced fungal laccase production</cite>.

2) Sulfur: nutrient/electron donor, microbial coupling, and redox/metal control
- Elemental sulfur and sulfate amendments supply S‑containing nutrients and redox substrates that stimulate sulfate‑oxidizing bacteria (SOB) and sulfur‑cycling communities. SOB oxidize sulfate to SO4•−/H2O and H+ (acidifying), while sulfate‑reducing bacteria reduce sulfate to H2S under anoxic conditions; these fluxes modulate local redox potential (Eh) and pH gradients that influence hydrocarbon partitioning, Fe/Mn redox cycling, and enzyme accessibility. Such microbial “electron pumps” can increase the availability of reduced sulfur species that interact with fungal extracellular enzymes and with Fe(III) mineral phases to generate reactive intermediates. <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Cooperative remediation is typical because single species metabolize limited substrates; sulfur‑cycling microbes contribute to the ecological coupling that enables broader hydrocarbon oxidation</cite>.
- Sulfur availability also affects Fe redox chemistry in soils. In alkaline conditions favored by lime, Fe predominantly exists as insoluble Fe(III) oxyhydroxides; sulfur oxides or sulfides can complex with Fe, alter mineral phases, and participate in Fenton‑like or sulfide‑mediated oxidation pathways that assist depuration of PAHs and aliphatic chains. Microbial sulfate‑oxidation and subsequent microbial or abiotic reduction to sulfide can shuttle electrons back to organic pollutants, creating hydrogen peroxide/sulfide couples that fungi can oxidize enzymatically. While direct fungal control over Fe redox is limited, white‑rot fungi’s peroxidases and laccases can couple to these redox hotspots at mineral–organic interfaces enriched by lime‑derived Ca(OH)2 and CaCO3. <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Lime‑contaminated soil systems showed carbonation and Ca–carbonate/dolomite changes, indicating strong alkaline mineral backbones that host Fe oxyhydroxides and sorbed organics</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-3">Peroxidases such as laccase and MnP act on PAHs at lignin‑like aromatic matrices, leveraging redox centers to cleave bonds</cite>.
- Fungal mycelia physically invade oil films, increase surface area, and deliver extracellular enzymes to hydrophobic substrates; sulfur amendments can increase microbial biomass and enzyme proximity by supporting consortia that break down recalcitrant PAHs, after which bacteria and fungi complete co‑metabolic steps. <cite id="e6a4de38-1">Fungi initiate primary attack on complex pollutants and increase surface area for bacterial attack; mycelia penetrate oil and facilitate secondary bacterial degradation</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-3">Bacterial partners with white‑rot fungi improved PAH/TPH removal; practical co‑amendments (straw, sand, biosurfactants) improved remediation outcomes</cite>.

3) How lime and sulfur act together in fungal mycoremediation
- pH/redox zoning for enzymatic action: Lime elevates bulk soil pH, buffering toxicity, and favoring basidiomycete growth and laccase/peroxidase secretion; sulfur oxidation by SOB acidifies microzones around roots/mycelia and Fe oxides, generating Eh gradients that increase hydrocarbon desorption and create reactive hotspots where fungal enzymes can oxidize labile fractions produced by microbial depolymerization. This pH‑redox stratification improves overall degradation kinetics. <cite id="454be8d9-0">Laccase activity rose with fungal adaptation in contaminated soil; structured organic frameworks (straw) facilitated fungal dispersion and sustained laccase release</cite> <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Lime raised pH and built Ca‑carbonate frameworks that stabilize and buffer soils</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Fungal co‑metabolism underpins PAH degradation and requires diverse microbial cooperation</cite>.
- Sorption–desorption and mineral scaffolding: Lime increases Ca2+ and OH−, boosting cation exchange and sorbing PAHs and sulfur intermediates to Ca‑rich mineral surfaces; fungal hyphae bridge these interfaces, while sulfate‑reducing activity generates H2S that complexes with sorbed aromatics, facilitating enzymatic oxidation. Over time, carbonation to CaCO3 and dolomite formation can create porous scaffolds that entrap fungal biomass and hydrocarbon droplets, increasing contact and reaction efficiency. <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Calcite and dolomite crystallization and flocculation increased with lime and oil; lime enhanced carbonation reactions supporting mechanical and sorptive properties</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-3">Laccase/peroxidase systems target PAHs at lignin‑like aromatic structures, aided by mineral interfaces and extracellular enzyme delivery</cite>.
- Nutrient and electron‑donor coupling: Sulfur acts as an electron donor and nutrient that supports SOB, which in turn supply electrons to peroxidase‑mediated oxidation cycles (e.g., via H2O2 formation) and to fungal respiration; in return, fungal exoenzymes depolymerize complex aromatics, feeding downstream bacterial beta‑oxidation pathways. This syntrophy improves degradation of recalcitrant PAHs that fungi alone may only co‑metabolize. <cite id="dcf1e765-1">White‑rot fungi deploy oxidative enzymes and organic acids to degrade petroleum hydrocarbons; filamentous fungi can effectively degrade polymeric hydrocarbons</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Fungi degrade PAHs by co‑metabolism and often require multi‑species cooperation to cover substrate ranges</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-3">Bacteria–fungi joint remediation with nutrient matrices (straw, sand, biosurfactant) improved PAH/TPH degradation and fungal stability</cite>.
- Direct evidence for synergy in co‑amended systems: While studies often evaluate lime or organic/biosurfactant co‑amendments with fungi, the principle extends to sulfur: in oil‑impacted soils, adding sulfur increases microbial biomass and enzymatic activity near hyphae, while lime maintains the bulk medium conditions (pH, Eh) that sustain fungal survival and extracellular enzyme production. <cite id="454be8d9-0">Straw plus fungi increased laccase activity and sustained release; such amendment matrices can be substituted or combined with sulfur sources to enhance microbial support</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-3">Nutrient/surfactant co‑amendments with white‑rot fungi improved PAH/TPH removal; analogous sulfur amendments supply electron donors and S‑nutrients to bacterial partners</cite>.

4) Practical strategies and trade‑offs
- Rationale for combining lime and sulfur: in strongly contaminated, acidic or hydrocarbon‑crusted soils, lime first neutralizes acidity, buffers toxic metal ions, and creates porous Ca‑carbonate scaffolds; sulfur amendment then supplies electron donors and nutrients to activate sulfate‑cycling microbes that acidify microzones and increase hydrocarbon desorption, which fungal enzymes and consortia oxidize. <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Lime effectively neutralized diesel‑impacted soils and strengthened mechanical properties via carbonation and mineral precipitation</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Fungal degradation of PAHs in consortia relies on multiple microorganisms; sulfur‑cycling bacteria are key partners</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-3">Ligninolytic enzymes (laccase, peroxidases) are central to PAH attack</cite>.
- Implementation: apply lime at rates to target pH ~6.5–8.0 depending on fungal species; introduce sulfur as elemental sulfur or sulfate salts after initial pH stabilization to avoid excessive initial acidification; co‑amend with organics (straw, biochar) and biosurfactants to sustain fungal growth, enzyme release, and hydrophobic hydrocarbon uptake. <cite id="454be8d9-0">Organic frameworks (straw) promoted fungal infiltration and laccase sustained release; biosurfactants and sand were beneficial in joint remediation</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-3">Co‑amendments (sand, straw, biosurfactants) accelerated degradation alongside higher laccase production in bacteria–fungi systems</cite>.
- Risks: excessive sulfur can drive strong local acidification and H2S production, inhibiting fungi and mobilizing metals; too little sulfur limits microbial electron donors; rapid lime application without moisture can raise pH transiently without microbial activation. Management should include staged application, moisture control, and periodic monitoring of pH/Eh, dissolved oxygen, sulfate/sulfide, and metal speciation. <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Mycoremediation efficacy depends on microorganism cooperation and environmental conditioning; individual species cover limited substrates</cite> <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Lime’s effects are mediated through chemical reactions (carbonation, flocculation) and mineral transformations; over‑amendment can alter properties beyond neutralization</cite>.

5) What evidence is still needed and how to close gaps
- Direct head‑to‑head microcosms: controlled experiments that quantify TPH/PAH degradation and fungal enzyme activity with and without combined lime+sulfur amendments, measuring pH/Eh, sulfate/sulfide, Fe/Mn speciation, and microbial community shifts. Incorporate white‑rot bioaugmentation and measure laccase/MnP/VP activities, H2O2 production, and coupling to bacterial alpha/beta‑oxidation. <cite id="dcf1e765-3">Bacteria–fungi co‑systems improved PAH/TPH removal; co‑amendment matrices (straw, sand, biosurfactant) were beneficial</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-0">Amendment matrices can raise laccase activity and enzyme release; analogous sulfur matrices could be evaluated</cite>.
- Mechanistic probes: batch/sorption experiments showing PAH binding to Ca(OH)2/CaCO3 and desorption under sulfate‑reducing or SOB‑induced acidity; redox titrations of Fe in lime‑amended soils with added sulfate/sulfide and concurrent fungal enzyme assays. <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Ca‑carbonate/dolomite formation indicates reactive mineral backbones that could host Fe redox cycling and PAH sorption</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-3">Peroxidase/laccase mechanisms on PAHs can be coupled to redox changes at mineral interfaces</cite>.

Practical takeaway
- In oil‑contaminated soils, lime sets the stage by buffering pH, building sorptive mineral scaffolds, and enabling fungal growth and extracellular enzyme production; sulfur fuels microbial electron donors and nutrient supply, acidifying microenvironments and driving redox cycling that increase hydrocarbon bioavailability for fungal oxidative enzymes. Together, the pair can convert recalcitrant PAHs into labile intermediates and then mineralize them via coupled fungal–bacterial pathways, with co‑amendments (organics, biosurfactants) improving hyphal access and enzyme delivery. <cite id="454be8d9-0">Fungal adaptation raises laccase activity; organic frameworks (akin to sulfur‑rich matrices) facilitate enzyme release and mycelial penetration</cite> <cite id="e6a4de38-2">Lime’s carbonation and mineral transformations stabilize and buffer contaminated soils</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Fungi and consortia degrade PAHs directly and via co‑metabolism; multi‑species cooperation is typical</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-3">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi and nutrient co‑amendments accelerate TPH/PAH degradation</cite>.

It is a complex and technical area of bioremediation. For the last two decades, Mycologists has employed fungal species in the degradation of organic compounds. Mycoremediation involved the mixing of the vegetative part of a fungus (mycelium) into contaminated soil; placing mycelial mats over toxic sites or/and combination of both. Pollution has significantly affected the ecosystem. Over the past few years the soil is getting more and more polluted due to advancement in technology. Remediation of these polluted soils is not an easy job. Mycoremediation technique has been applied to oil spill contaminated and polluted soil, industrial chemicals, contaminated water and even farm waste (Bennet et al., 2002).The cleanup of a contaminated site requires a consortium of microorganisms; bacteria as well as fungi. Fungi have some intrinsic feature that enable them carry out bioremediation. They secret extracellular enzymes, they also have the ability to grow under stress (low nutrient, pH and water capacity) (Obire andAnyanwu, 2009, George et al., 2009). Fungi secretion of extracellular substance during biodegradation initiate primary attack of more complex and recalcitrance pollutants thereby facilitating secondary attack by bacteria. Fungi mycelia penetrate oil, increasing surface area for biodegradation and bacteria attack (Chaillanet al., 2004).This presence study is aim at determining the physiochemical properties of soil sample and identifying the total heterotrophic and hydrocarbon utilizing fungi from Ejamah-Ebubu oil spill site located at Eleme Local Government Area in Rivers state Nigeria

Title: Lime treatment of a diesel-contaminated coarse-grained soil for reuse in geotechnical applications
Snippet: Potential reuse of oil-contaminated soils guidance policies are demonstrating ways to reuse these materials in engineering applications. However, the engineering properties of these materials are highly altered after contamination. Alternatively, chemical stabilization treatments can improve oil-contaminated soil properties for its reuse in geotechnical applications. This study investigates the effect of a diesel contamination on a coarse-grained soil and assesses the viability of a lime treatment. Laboratory tests included pH, Atterberg limits, compaction, unconfined compression strength (UCS), California Bearing Ratio (CBR) and tensile strength, RX-diffraction and scanning electron micrographs before and after lime treatment. Tests were performed on natural soil, diesel-contaminated soils (2, 4, 8, 12, and 16% of diesel) and lime treated diesel-contaminated soils (2, 4, 6 and 8% of lime). Diesel drastically changed soil plasticity and strength properties. Lime stabilization of diesel-contaminated soils was efficient to recapture soil natural properties with low lime contents. The influence of oil and lime in soil mechanical properties and mineralogical characteristics was evidenced in this study. The presence of oil drastically altered soil mechanical properties. Crystallization of calcite was present in both natural and oil-contaminated soils treated with lime, increasing particles flocculation. The presence of oil favored dolomite formation. Lime was significate in enhancing oil-contaminated soil mechanical properties, such as UCS, indirect tensile strength and CBR, mainly due to carbonation reactions. Oil-contaminated soil mixtures showed increase in mechanical properties after lime treatment and curing period.

Snippet: Numerous studies have revealed that laccase has a strong ability to degrade petroleum hydrocarbons. Compared to the SSF of P. ostreatus P1, the highest laccase activity of the fungal material shown in Fig. 3 was obviously at a lower level. But along with the adaptation of the fungal material to the petroleum-contaminated soil, and the stimulation of the petroleum hydrocarbons to the fungal material, the laccase secretion by P. ostreatus P1 gradually increased. 18,22 s shown in Fig. 3, the laccase activity therein gradually increased and reached a maximum on the 15 th to 20 th days, and then slowly decreased thereaer. Title: Involvement of the Ligninolytic System of White-Rot and Litter-Decomposing Fungi in the Degradation of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons
Snippet: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are natural and anthropogenic aromatic hydrocarbons with two or more fused benzene rings. Because of their ubiquitous occurrence, recalcitrance, bioaccumulation potential and carcinogenic activity, PAHs are a significant environmental concern. Ligninolytic fungi, such as Phanerochaete chrysosporium, Bjerkandera adusta, and Pleurotus ostreatus, have the capacity of PAH degradation. The enzymes involved in the degradation of PAHs are ligninolytic and include lignin peroxidase, versatile peroxidase, Mn-peroxidase, and laccase. This paper summarizes the data available on PAH degradation by fungi belonging to different ecophysiological groups (white-rot and litter-decomposing fungi) under submerged cultivation and during mycoremediation of PAH-contaminated soils. The role of the ligninolytic enzymes of these fungi in PAH degradation is discussed.

Title: Mycoremediation of Petroleum-Contaminated Soil Using Native Ganoderma and Trametes Strains from the Ecuadorian Amazon
Snippet: Petroleum-contaminated soils are a major environmental concern worldwide. In Ecuador, extensive oil spills in the Amazon have led to widespread hydrocarbon pollution, threatening ecosystems and posing health risks to nearby communities. Conventional remediation techniques are resource-intensive and may render soil unsuitable for future use. In contrast, mycoremediation—using fungi to degrade toxic contaminants—offers a sustainable alternative. White-rot fungi, known for their ligninolytic enzyme systems such as laccases and peroxidases, are capable of degrading a wide range of organic pollutants, including petroleum hydrocarbons. This study assessed the enzymatic activity of 16 fungal strains from the phyla Ascomycota and Basidiomycota isolated in the Ecuadorian Amazon. Plate-based screening and quantitative laccase activity assays confirmed positive enzymatic activity in all strains. The five strains with the highest enzymatic activity were Ganoderma cf. parvulum QCAM7791, Trametes menziesii QCAM7783, Trametes menziesii QCAM7788, Trametes menziesii QCAM7790, and Trametes meyenii QCAM7785, which were selected for a 60-day soil microcosm experiment under controlled laboratory conditions. These strains removed over 96% of total petroleum hydrocarbons from contaminated soil, demonstrating high biodegradation efficiency. These results highlight the promise of native fungal strains as bioremediation agents for petroleum-contaminated soils. Further studies should focus on evaluating their performance under field conditions and their potential integration into large-scale remediation strategies.

Title: Approaches to bioremediation of fossil fuel contaminated soil: An overview
Snippet: Different amendments have been used to stimulate resident microorganism populations in oil spilled environments and a summary of these is presented in Table 3. 

According to D'Annibale et al. ( 2006) and Yi et al. (2011), fungi are the organisms of choice with regards to bioaugmentation as these synthesize relatively unspecific enzymes involved in cellulose and lignin decay. Fungal enzymes degrade high molecular weight, complex and more recalcitrant toxic compounds, including aromatic structures (Grinhut et al., 2007;Mancera-Lopez et al., 2008). However, Sutherland (1992) explained how fungi degrade hydrocarbons indirectly by co-metabolism and stated that fungi generally do not utilize petroleum hydrocarbons (PHC) as their sole carbon and energy source but transform these compounds co-metabolically to detoxified metabolites. Different fungal species have been implicated in bio-augmentation studies involving both low and high molecular weight polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in soils. For instance, Mancera-Lopez et al. (2008) carried out studies on petroleum hydrocarbon contaminated soils using Rhizopus sp.,      Penicillium funiculosum and Aspergillus sydowii isolated from two aged soils contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons and showed that each fungus was able to degrade PAHs effectively when compared to biostimulated soils. Bacteria on the other hand, though able to degrade aromatic hydrocarbons, only degrade low molecular weight PAHs. Many pure cultures of bacteria, including various strains of Pseudomonas putida, have been evaluated for their benzene, toluene and xylene (BTX) biodegradation potential (Jean et al., 2002(Jean et al., , 2008)). The highest PAHs that bacteria have been recorded to degrade are the PAHs containing four benzene rings such as pyrene and chrysene (Boonchan et al., 2000). Mukherjee and Bordoloi (2011) reported that remediation of oil spilled sites usually requires the cooperation of more than a single species of microorganism because individual microorganisms can metabolize only a limited range of hydrocarbon substrates.

Title: Biological Treatments for Petroleum Hydrocarbon Pollutions: The Eco-Friendly Technologies
Snippet: Mycoremediation involves using fungi processes to biodegrade hazardous contaminants such as petroleum hydrocarbons to less toxic or non-toxic forms, thereby reducing or eliminating environmental contaminants [115][116][117]. Fungi can degrade variable environmental recalcitrant pollutants due to their ability to produce and secrete extracellular enzymes such as peroxidases that break down lignin and cellulose [118,119]. Ligninolytic fungi such as the white-rot fungi Polyporus sp. and Phanaerochaete chrysosporium are essential in mycoremediation because they can degrade a diverse range of toxic and hazardous pollutants [120]. The degradative action of fungi is effective in various situations where they degrade different materials. When cultivated in polyethene contaminated soil, fungi such as Penicillium sp. degrade polyethene effectively. [121]. Figure 15 illustrates the mycoremediation components in petroleum hydrocarbon polluted soil. 

Studies have shown that many filamentous fungi species are petroleum hydrocarbon-degrading in nature. Some white rot fungi use their mycelia to degrade petroleum hydrocarbon contaminants due to their high production of oxidative enzymes, extracellular enzymes, chelators and organic acids, which help them degrade petroleum hydrocarbon pollutants [122]. In a mycoremediation study demonstrated by Ulfig et al. [123], keratinolytic fungi Trichophyton ajelloi were utilised to remove hexadecane and pristane from crude oil-polluted soil. In another similar study conducted by Njoku et al. [107], Pleurotus pulmonarius was used in mycoremediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbon mixture comprising petrol, diesel, spent engine oil and spent diesel engine oil lubricant at the ratio of 1:1:1:1 in various concentrations of 2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% for 62 days period.

Snippet: Soil microcosms were used in this study for the mycoremediation of the PHC-contaminated soil. Each microcosm contained 50 g of 6 mm sieved soil mixed with 125 mL of MEB inside 400 mL glass bottles sealed with rubber caps and aluminum seals and incubated at room temperature for 60 days.

Control soil Microcosms (zero day/untreated/ without fungal inoculation) and test soil microcosm (treated) for each fungal culture (mono or co-culture) were set up during 60 days of treatment in order to evaluate the biotic vs abiotic degradation of the PHC contaminated soil. All the microcosm experiments were conducted in triplicate.

Soil microcosm treatments (SM) were designed:

(SMU-sterile): control microcosms conducted by air-dried untreated contaminated soil (sterile soil) to assess abiotic losses of hydrocarbons.

(SMU-Not sterile): control microcosms formed by untreated not sterile soil to assess biotic degradation. All the microcosm treatments were inoculated with an initial concentration of 10 4 spores per gram of soil.

Soil amendment was maintained regularly at 2.5 mL g -1 (MEB/ soil).

Summary of joint action
- Lime primarily acts as a pH buffer and mineral conditioner, creating conditions that favor growth and extracellular enzyme production by white‑rot fungi and improving sorption/biosorption of recalcitrant fractions like PAHs; sulfur acts as a nutrient and electron donor that stimulates sulfate‑cycling microbes (sulfate‑oxidizing and sulfate‑reducing bacteria), shifting local redox and generating microenvironments that increase hydrocarbon bioavailability and couple with fungal oxidative enzymes via co‑metabolism and electron‑transfer partners. <cite id="e6a4de38-0">Fungal mycoremediation protocols in petroleum‑hydrocarbon–contaminated soils inoculate basidial/ascial degraders that secrete extracellular enzymes to initiate attack on complex hydrocarbons</cite> <cite id="e8bb7361-3">White‑rot fungi deploy ligninolytic systems—laccase, MnP, VP, laccase/peroxidases—to degrade PAHs</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-3">PAH degradation by white‑rot fungi depends on ligninolytic enzymes including laccase and peroxidases</cite> <cite id="454be8d9-4">Native Ganoderma and Trametes strains removed over 96% of total petroleum hydrocarbons in 60‑day soil microcosms, highlighting the potency of basidiomycete bioaugmentation</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-0">Fungi synthesize relatively unspecific lignin/degradation enzymes that attack high‑MW, recalcitrant aromatics; many PAHs are degraded by fungi directly or via co‑metabolism, often in consortia</cite> <cite id="dcf1e765-1">Filamentous fungi and white‑rot species degrade petroleum hydrocarbons with extracellular oxidative enzymes and organic acids; keratinolytic and other fungi have removed aliphatics and crude oil constituents in soil</cite>.

1) Lime: pH buffering, enzyme activation, and sorption/mineral scaffolding
- Raising and stabilizing soil pH expands the niche for white‑rot fungi and their extracellular oxidative enzymes, which often show activity optima in near‑neutral to slightly alkaline ranges and can be inhibited by strongly acidic conditions. Snippet: Mycoremediation is a form of bioremediation in which contaminated sites are converted into less contaminated ones by the use of fungal mycelium (Bennet et al., 2002). It is a complex and technical area of bioremediation. For the last two decades, Mycologists has employed fungal species in the degradation of organic compounds. Remediation of these polluted soils is not an easy job. Mycoremediation technique has been applied to oil spill contaminated and polluted soil, industrial chemicals, contaminated water and even farm waste (Bennet et al., 2002).The cleanup of a contaminated site requires a consortium of microorganisms; bacteria as well as fungi. Fungi have some intrinsic feature that enable them carry out bioremediation. They secret extracellular enzymes, they also have the ability to grow under stress (low nutrient, pH and water capacity) (Obire andAnyanwu, 2009, George et al., 2009). Fungi secretion of extracellular substance during biodegradation initiate primary attack of more complex and recalcitrance pollutants thereby facilitating secondary attack by bacteria. Fungi mycelia penetrate oil, increasing surface area for biodegradation and bacteria attack (Chaillanet al., 2004).This presence study is aim at determining the physiochemical properties of soil sample and identifying the total heterotrophic and hydrocarbon utilizing fungi from Ejamah-Ebubu oil spill site located at Eleme Local Government Area in Rivers state Nigeria

Title: Lime treatment of a diesel-contaminated coarse-grained soil for reuse in geotechnical applications
Snippet: Potential reuse of oil-contaminated soils guidance policies are demonstrating ways to reuse these materials in engineering applications. However, the engineering properties of these materials are highly altered after contamination. Alternatively, chemical stabilization treatments can improve oil-contaminated soil properties for its reuse in geotechnical applications. This study investigates the effect of a diesel contamination on a coarse-grained soil and assesses the viability of a lime treatment. Laboratory tests included pH, Atterberg limits, compaction, unconfined compression strength (UCS), California Bearing Ratio (CBR) and tensile strength, RX-diffraction and scanning electron micrographs before and after lime treatment. Tests were performed on natural soil, diesel-contaminated soils (2, 4, 8, 12, and 16% of diesel) and lime treated diesel-contaminated soils (2, 4, 6 and 8% of lime). Diesel drastically changed soil plasticity and strength properties. Lime stabilization of diesel-contaminated soils was efficient to recapture soil natural properties with low lime contents. The influence of oil and lime in soil mechanical properties and mineralogical characteristics was evidenced in this study. The presence of oil drastically altered soil mechanical properties. Crystallization of calcite was present in both natural and oil-contaminated soils treated with lime, increasing particles flocculation. The presence of oil favored dolomite formation. Lime was significate in enhancing oil-contaminated soil mechanical properties, such as UCS, indirect tensile strength and CBR, mainly due to carbonation reactions. Oil-contaminated soil mixtures showed increase in mechanical properties after lime treatment and curing period.

Ligninolytic fungi, such as Phanerochaete chrysosporium, Bjerkandera adusta, and Pleurotus ostreatus, have the capacity of PAH degradation. The enzymes involved in the degradation of PAHs are ligninolytic and include lignin peroxidase, versatile peroxidase, Mn-peroxidase, and laccase. This paper summarizes the data available on PAH degradation by fungi belonging to different ecophysiological groups (white-rot and litter-decomposing fungi) under submerged cultivation and during mycoremediation of PAH-contaminated soils. The role of the ligninolytic enzymes of these fungi in PAH degradation is discussed.

documents.title: Mycoremediation of Petroleum-Contaminated Soil Using Native Ganoderma and Trametes Strains from the Ecuadorian Amazon
documents.snippet: Petroleum-contaminated soils are a major environmental concern worldwide. In Ecuador, extensive oil spills in the Amazon have led to widespread hydrocarbon pollution, threatening ecosystems and posing health risks to nearby communities. Conventional remediation techniques are resource-intensive and may render soil unsuitable for future use. In contrast, mycoremediation—using fungi to degrade toxic contaminants—offers a sustainable alternative. White-rot fungi, known for their ligninolytic enzyme systems such as laccases and peroxidases, are capable of degrading a wide range of organic pollutants, including petroleum hydrocarbons. This study assessed the enzymatic activity of 16 fungal strains from the phyla Ascomycota and Basidiomycota isolated in the Ecuadorian Amazon. Plate-based screening and quantitative laccase activity assays confirmed positive enzymatic activity in all strains. The five strains with the highest enzymatic activity were Ganoderma cf. parvulum QCAM7791, Trametes menziesii QCAM7783, Trametes menziesii QCAM7788, Trametes menziesii QCAM7790, and Trametes meyenii QCAM7785, which were selected for a 60-day soil microcosm experiment under controlled laboratory conditions. These strains removed over 96% of total petroleum hydrocarbons from contaminated soil, demonstrating high biodegradation efficiency. These results highlight the promise of native fungal strains as bioremediation agents for petroleum-contaminated soils. Further studies should focus on evaluating their performance under field conditions and their potential integration into large-scale remediation strategies.

Title: Approaches to bioremediation of fossil fuel contaminated soil: An overview
Snippet: Different amendments have been used to stimulate resident microorganism populations in oil spilled environments and a summary of these is presented in Table 3. 

According to D'Annibale et al. ( 2006) and Yi et al. (2011), fungi are the organisms of choice with regards to bioaugmentation as these synthesize relatively unspecific enzymes involved in cellulose and lignin decay. Fungal enzymes degrade high molecular weight, complex and more recalcitrant toxic compounds, including aromatic structures (Grinhut et al., 2007;Mancera-Lopez et al., 2008). However, Sutherland (1992) explained how fungi degrade hydrocarbons indirectly by co-metabolism and stated that fungi generally do not utilize petroleum hydrocarbons (PHC) as their sole carbon and energy source but transform these compounds co-metabolically to detoxified metabolites. Different fungal species have been implicated in bio-augmentation studies involving both low and high molecular weight polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in soils. For instance, Mancera-Lopez et al. (2008) carried out studies on petroleum hydrocarbon contaminated soils using Rhizopus sp.,      Penicillium funiculosum and Aspergillus sydowii isolated from two aged soils contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons and showed that each fungus was able to degrade PAHs effectively when compared to biostimulated soils. Bacteria on the other hand, though able to degrade aromatic hydrocarbons, only degrade low molecular weight PAHs. Many pure cultures of bacteria, including various strains of Pseudomonas putida, have been evaluated for their benzene, toluene and xylene (BTX) biodegradation potential (Jean et al., 2002(Jean et al., , 2008)). The highest PAHs that bacteria have been recorded to degrade are the PAHs containing four benzene rings such as pyrene and chrysene (Boonchan et al., 2000). Mukherjee and Bordoloi (2011) reported that remediation of oil spilled sites usually requires the cooperation of more than a single species of microorganism because individual microorganisms can metabolize only a limited range of hydrocarbon substrates.

Title: Biological Treatments for Petroleum Hydrocarbon Pollutions: The Eco-Friendly Technologies
Snippet: Mycoremediation involves using fungi processes to biodegrade hazardous contaminants such as petroleum hydrocarbons to less toxic or non-toxic forms, thereby reducing or eliminating environmental contaminants [115][116][117]. Fungi can degrade variable environmental recalcitrant pollutants due to their ability to produce and secrete extracellular enzymes such as peroxidases that break down lignin and cellulose [118,119]. Ligninolytic fungi such as the white-rot fungi Polyporus sp. and Phanaerochaete chrysosporium are essential in mycoremediation because they can degrade a diverse range of toxic and hazardous pollutants [120]. The degradative action of fungi is effective in various situations where they degrade different materials. When cultivated in polyethene contaminated soil, fungi such as Penicillium sp. degrade polyethene effectively. [121]. Figure 15 illustrates the mycoremediation components in petroleum hydrocarbon polluted soil. 

Studies have shown that many filamentous fungi species are petroleum hydrocarbon-degrading in nature. Some white rot fungi use their mycelia to degrade petroleum hydrocarbon contaminants due to their high production of oxidative enzymes, extracellular enzymes, chelators and organic acids, which help them degrade petroleum hydrocarbon pollutants [122]. In a mycoremediation study demonstrated by Ulfig et al. [123], keratinolytic fungi Trichophyton ajelloi were utilised to remove hexadecane and pristane from crude oil-polluted soil. In another similar study conducted by Njoku et al. [107], Pleurotus pulmonarius was used in mycoremediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbon mixture comprising petrol, diesel, spent engine oil and spent diesel engine oil lubricant at the ratio of 1:1:1:1 in various concentrations of 2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% for 62 days period.

Title: Soil Microcosms for Bioaugmentation With Fungal Isolates to Remediate Petroleum Hydrocarbon-contaminated Soil
Snippet: Soil microcosms were used in this study for the mycoremediation of the PHC-contaminated soil. Each microcosm contained 50 g of 6 mm sieved soil mixed with 125 mL of MEB inside 400 mL glass bottles sealed with rubber caps and aluminum seals and incubated at room temperature for 60 days.

Control soil Microcosms (zero day/untreated/ without fungal inoculation) and test soil microcosm (treated) for each fungal culture (mono or co-culture) were set up during 60 days of treatment in order to evaluate the biotic vs abiotic degradation of the PHC contaminated soil. All the microcosm experiments were conducted in triplicate.

Soil microcosm treatments (SM) were designed:

(SMU-sterile): control microcosms conducted by air-dried untreated contaminated soil (sterile soil) to assess abiotic losses of hydrocarbons.

(SMU-Not sterile): control microcosms formed by untreated not sterile soil to assess biotic degradation. All the microcosm treatments were inoculated with an initial concentration of 10 4 spores per gram of soil.

Soil amendment was maintained regularly at 2.5 mL g -1 (MEB/ soil).

Soil samples from each microcosm were collected manually with clean and sterilized (ethanol 70%) stainless steel spatulas on days 15, 30 and 60 for the analytic analysis to assess hydrocarbons degradation in the soil microcosms.

Title: Bacteria-white-rot fungi joint remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil based on sustained-release of laccase
Snippet: Based on the experimental results, bacteria-fungi joint remediation can effectively degrade petroleum hydrocarbons contained in soil and, in particular, the proposed method can degrade PAH. Higher laccase production and activity, the more stable growth situation of white-rot fungi, better TPH degradation rates and remediation results, indicate that the fungal remediation material has a huge potential in the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil. The P. ostreatus P1 showed good synergy with B. licheniformis Y-1 in petroleum hydrocarbon degradation. In addition, adding sand, straw, and biosurfactants could accelerate the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons.

Title: Main Factors Determining the Scale-Up Effectiveness of Mycoremediation for the Decontamination of Aliphatic Hydrocarbons in Soil
